title: As the deer (Psalm 42)
hookLine: as a deer pants for water; why are you cast down, my soul?
carry: why so cast down, my soul?
last: THE MEEK SHALL INHERIT THE EARTH.

cards: The stream bed is mostly stones now. A deer comes down the hillside to the place where the water ran in spring, and stands there, sides heaving, nose low, searching. It knows exactly what it needs.

Now set a person beside that deer: someone who used to walk with the crowd on feast days, singing all the way up to the house of God, and who now lives far away, while the people around him ask, so where's your God now?
Today's psalm opens with that deer. Then the writer turns around and starts talking to his own soul.

teach.h: A HART AT THE WATER BROOKS
teach.b: Psalm forty-two begins, in the King James Bible: "As the hart panteth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul after thee, O God."

The Hebrew for those brooks means channels of water, the kind that run full in the rainy season and can shrink to nothing in a dry one, so some readers picture an animal hunting for water that's hard to find.
Its heading gives it to the sons of Korah, a family of temple singers. The writer remembers leading the crowds to the house of God with shouts of joy.

teach.h: TEARS FOR FOOD, DAY AND NIGHT
teach.b: Now he's far off, by the Jordan and the slopes of Mount Hermon, and he says: "My tears have been my meat day and night, while they continually say unto me, Where is thy God?" Meat, in older English, simply meant food.
He has been living on tears. Then the turn.

teach.h: WHY ART THOU CAST DOWN, O MY SOUL?
teach.b: He speaks to himself: "Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted in me? hope thou in God." He asks his own sadness a question, then gives it a gentle instruction. Not snap out of it.
Hope. The same lines come back three times, twice here and once in Psalm forty-three, one reason some readers treat the two psalms as a single poem.
And between the refrains, the sadness doesn't vanish: "Deep calleth unto deep," he says, every wave going over his head.

teach.h: THIRST IS A MEASURE OF WANTING
teach.b: In this psalm, thirst isn't a failure of faith.
It's a measure of how much someone wants God.

how: Some Christians turn to Psalm 42 in seasons of spiritual dryness, grief or homesickness; it is chanted in monastic daily prayer and sung in hymn versions such as "As pants the hart for cooling streams."

games.q: you're far from the place you used to worship, and people keep asking where your God is. you feel low. what do you do?
o: pretend you're fine and change the subject.
ask your own soul why it's cast down, and tell it to hope.

games.why: the psalmist talks to himself: "why art thou cast down, O my soul? … hope thou in God." not a lecture, a question and then hope.

practice: Notice what is low in you today, tiredness, a worry, missing someone, and don't push it away. Ask it the psalm's question quietly, the way you'd ask a friend who looked down: why so cast down?
Answer it gently, without a lecture; if you pray, add the psalm's own words, hope thou in God, and if you don't, just keep your soul company for a while.

wordCard.voice: Hart. The old English word for a male deer, the thirsty animal Psalm forty-two compares to a soul longing for God.
